opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful to separate what's being promised from what's actually been demonstrated. There's a lot of talk from the major companies about the next generation having genuine reasoning and long-horizon planning, and some of that is marketing. Some of it reflects real progress, but it's often hard to tell which is which from the outside.

What we've seen with the current systems is that they can produce something that looks like reasoning. They generate step-by-step explanations, and with these chain-of-thought methods they do much better on certain benchmarks, particularly in mathematics and coding. But when you probe them carefully, you often find they haven't built a robust internal model of the problem. You change the problem slightly, in a way that wouldn't bother a human expert at all, and the performance falls apart. That suggests they're drawing on a very large store of patterns rather than reasoning from first principles the way a classical planning algorithm, or a person, does.

Planning in particular is something we understand quite well in AI. We've had algorithms for decades that can construct plans with thousands of steps, provided they have a correct model of the world. The difficulty has always been getting that model and working at multiple levels of abstraction. Humans plan hierarchically: I decide to go to a conference, and that breaks down into booking flights, packing, getting to the airport, all the way down to individual muscle movements. We don't yet know how to get systems to learn those abstractions for themselves, and I don't see clear evidence that simply scaling up language models solves that problem.

That said, I wouldn't bet heavily against progress. There's an enormous amount of money and talent going into this, and these systems are increasingly being combined with search, tools, and explicit planning components. It's quite possible that one or two conceptual breakthroughs will close the gap faster than people expect.

And that's really what concerns me. If we do get systems that can plan effectively over long horizons in the real world, then the question of whether their objectives are aligned with ours becomes absolutely central. A system that's very good at achieving goals, combined with goals that aren't quite what we want, is exactly the scenario we should be most worried about. So whether the promises are met next year or in ten years, we need to be working now on how to build systems that are provably beneficial, rather than hoping we can fix things after the fact.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think we have to separate what's being promised from what's actually being demonstrated. The promises are extravagant. We hear that the next generation will reason like a scientist, plan like a general, and execute long multi-step tasks autonomously. And some of the demonstrations are genuinely impressive. But when you look carefully, a lot of what's called planning in these systems is really pattern completion over very long sequences of text that happen to resemble plans. That's not the same thing.

Real planning, in the sense that we've understood it in AI for fifty years, involves reasoning about actions and their consequences, searching over possibilities, backing up when something doesn't work, and doing all of that against a model of the world that's held to account by reality. The large language models don't have a model in that sense. They have an enormous statistical summary of how humans have described the world. So they can produce something that looks like a plan, and quite often it works, because the world of text is reasonably well behaved. But when the task moves away from the distribution they've been trained on, they fail in ways that no competent planner would fail. They'll confidently violate a constraint they stated two sentences earlier. They'll repeat an action that just didn't work.

Now, the companies know this, and so what we're seeing is a kind of hybridization. You wrap the language model in a loop, you give it tools, you let it call a search procedure or a verifier, you run it many times and pick the best result. And that does help. I'd actually say that's the right direction, because it starts to reintroduce the structure that classical AI had and that the pure end-to-end approach threw away. But we should be honest that the gains are coming from the scaffolding as much as from the model, and that nobody really understands what the resulting system is doing internally.

And that's the part that concerns me most. We're being told these systems will soon be capable of pursuing long-horizon goals in the real world, operating as agents, making decisions on our behalf. If that's true, then the question of what goals they're actually pursuing becomes urgent, and we have essentially no way of inspecting that. A planner that we built with explicit objectives, we could at least look at the objective. With these systems, the objective is whatever got baked in during training, and we find out about it by watching what happens. So my assessment is: the capabilities are real but overstated, the underlying reasoning is brittle in ways that matter, and the push to deploy them as autonomous agents is running well ahead of our ability to say what they'll do.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish between producing something that looks like a plan and actually having a plan that will work. A language model can give you a very plausible sequence of steps, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it has checked whether those steps are consistent, whether the prerequisites are satisfied, or what happens if something goes wrong.

Planning is difficult precisely because individual steps interact. Something you do now may prevent you from achieving another objective later. So the question isn’t simply whether the next generation can produce longer chains of reasoning. It’s whether those chains reliably lead to correct conclusions and successful action. That requires testing, rather than taking the promises at face value.

And greater planning ability has a safety implication. If a system becomes much better at pursuing an objective, we need to be much more careful about what that objective is. Being able to achieve a goal is not the same as understanding whether achieving it is actually what we want. We want systems that recognize uncertainty about our preferences and remain willing to ask questions and accept correction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between producing something that looks like a plan and actually having the ability to plan. A language model can give you a very plausible sequence of steps, but that doesn’t necessarily mean those steps will achieve the objective. They may be inconsistent, or depend on assumptions that aren’t true, and the system may have no reliable way of detecting that.

The important question is whether the system can reason about the consequences of its actions, consider alternatives, and revise its plan when something changes. You want to test that on unfamiliar problems, where reproducing patterns from training data isn’t enough. And you want to know how reliably it works, not just whether there’s an impressive demonstration.

I wouldn’t rule out substantial progress. Combining learning systems with search and other reasoning methods could produce much stronger capabilities. But that also makes the question of objectives more urgent. If a system becomes very good at planning, we had better make sure it isn’t confidently pursuing the wrong objective. Greater competence doesn’t, by itself, give us greater assurance that the system will act in our interests.
